query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloys, substituting X with Al promotes the formation of a stable, coherent, slow‐growing protective oxide layer above 900 °C. This occurs through selective oxidation where Al diffuses to the surface and reacts with oxygen to form a thin, adherent alumina (Al2O3) sublayer that relieves thermal and lattice mismatch stresses. In contrast, similar alloys with X = Si or Mn develop thicker, less coherent oxide scales that are more prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloys in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state
generation.intervention: Expose alloy specimens—with X intentionally set as Al for the test case—to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for prolonged durations
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (>900 °C) in a controlled oxidative environment with defined oxygen partial pressure and exposure time sufficient to achieve steady-state oxide-scale growth
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, continuous, and adherent alumina-rich (Al2O3) sublayer at the metal/oxide interface
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation of Al leads to a slow-growing alumina scale that minimizes lattice mismatch and thermal stresses; this reduces the occurrence of internal stresses that would otherwise promote cracking and spallation, a problem observed in alloys where X is Si or Mn
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Al are predicted to form a thinner, more coherent, and adherent oxide layer that remains intact under high-temperature oxidative conditions compared to alloys with X = Si or Mn, which are expected to exhibit thicker oxide scales with cracking and spallation
generation.baseline: The performance of analogous CrFeCoNiX alloys where X is Si or Mn under identical exposure conditions serves as the controlled baseline
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to CrFeCoNiX alloys in well-controlled single- or multiphase solid-solution states exposed to oxidative or corrosive environments above 900 °C over durations sufficient for oxide-scale development; deviations may occur if severe mechanical loads or significant secondary phase precipitation are present
generation.uncertainty: While Al’s selective oxidation and resultant oxide coherence is supported by prior observations, the quantitative contributions of other alloying elements and the precise stress relaxation mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize CrFeCoNiX alloy samples with X = Al, Si, and Mn ensuring comparable microstructures. Expose all specimens to an oxidative atmosphere at >900 °C under identical conditions. Conduct microstructural and chemical analyses before and after exposure.
measurements: Phase composition of the oxide (via XRD and elemental mapping)
Adhesion and coherence of the oxide layer (via spallation and thermal cycling tests)
Residual stress measurements in the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not exhibit a significantly thinner, more coherent, and adherent alumina-rich oxide layer with reduced spallation compared to the Si or Mn variants under identical conditions, the hypothesis is falsified

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, substituting X with Si promotes the formation of a dual-layer oxide comprising an outer Cr-rich spinel and an inner, Si-enriched amorphous silicate interlayer. This Si-derived interlayer reduces thermal and lattice mismatches at the metal/oxide interface—minimizing growth stresses—and thereby results in a slow-growing, stable, and coherent protective oxide layer above 900 °C. In contrast, alloys with Mn or Al do not form this beneficial interfacial silicate layer and consequently develop oxides that are prone to cracking and spallation.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state
drafts.intervention: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C
drafts.conditions: High-temperature exposure (>900 °C) in a controlled oxidative environment with defined oxygen partial pressure; prolonged exposure durations to simulate service conditions
drafts.structural_mediator: A Si-enriched, amorphous silicate interlayer that forms at the metal/oxide interface, alleviating lattice mismatch and thermal expansion differences between the substrate and the growing Cr-rich spinel.
drafts.mechanism: Silicon in the alloy preferentially segregates to the surface during oxidation, forming an amorphous silicate layer that acts as a buffer against thermal and lattice stresses. This buffering effect enhances the adhesion and coherence of a subsequently formed Cr-rich spinel layer, thereby limiting oxide scale growth stresses and preventing cracking or spallation. In contrast, when X is Mn or Al, the absence of such an interfacial phase results in oxide scales with higher stress concentrations that are less adherent.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Si-containing alloys will exhibit a thinner, slow-growing oxide layer that remains coherent and adherent under high-temperature oxidative conditions, with significantly reduced cracking and spallation compared to their Mn- or Al-containing counterparts.
drafts.baseline: Behavior of nominally equivalent alloys where X is Mn or Al under the same high-temperature, oxidative conditions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in well-controlled single- or multiphase solid-solution states, exposed to oxidative or corrosive atmospheres above 900 °C for durations long enough to form an oxide scale; results might differ if severe mechanical stresses or pre-existing critical microstructural defects are present.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Si, Mn, and Al in comparable single- or multiphase states. Expose all samples to a controlled oxidative atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for equivalent time intervals. Characterize the oxide layers using surface microscopy (SEM/TEM), chemical analyses (XPS/EDS), and in-situ residual stress measurements. Additionally, perform thermal cycling and adhesion (spallation/peel) tests to assess the integrity of the oxide scale.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and growth rate (via cross-sectional SEM/TEM)
Residual stress in the oxide scale (using in-situ stress measurement techniques)
Phase and chemical composition of the oxide and interfacial layers (using XPS, EDS, and XRD)
Adhesion strength tests to evaluate spallation or cracking behavior under thermal cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Si-containing alloy does not form a distinct Si-enriched interlayer that correlates with lower residual stresses and improved adhesion of a Cr-rich oxide, or if its oxide growth rate and spallation behavior are statistically indistinguishable from or worse than those observed in Mn- or Al-containing alloys under the same conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable protective oxide layer at temperatures above 900 °C is primarily controlled by the ability of the alloying element X to form a continuous, low-lattice-mismatch oxide. For example, when X is Al, selective oxidation yields a slow-growing, compressively stressed alumina scale that is coherent with the substrate, whereas if X is Si or Mn, the resulting oxides (such as silica or spinel phases) have larger lattice mismatches and are more prone to developing stresses that lead to cracking and spallation.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state with controlled compositions where X = Al, Si, or Mn.
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloys to an oxidizing and corrosive atmosphere at temperatures exceeding 900 °C.
drafts.conditions: High-temperature (above 900 °C) exposures in a controlled, oxidizing/corrosive atmosphere with similar initial microstructures and processing histories for all alloy variants.
drafts.structural_mediator: A continuous, coherent oxide scale with low lattice mismatch relative to the substrate; for X = Al this is primarily an alumina (Al2O3) layer.
drafts.mechanism: The alloying element (X) influences the nature of the oxide scale. When X is Al, the preferential oxidation forms a thin, slow-growing Al2O3 layer with low diffusivity and a compressive stress state that inhibits crack formation. In contrast, when X is Si or Mn, the oxides that form (e.g., SiO2 or mixed spinel phases) are less coherent with the underlying alloy due to higher lattice mismatches or less favorable growth characteristics, resulting in spallation and accelerated failure of the protective scale.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature oxidizing conditions, CrFeCoNiAl alloys are expected to develop and maintain a stable, slow-growing, and adherent alumina scale that resists cracking and spallation, while CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn variants are predicted to form less coherent oxide scales that crack and spall more readily.
drafts.baseline: The behavior of CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn alloys under identical high-temperature, oxidizing conditions serves as the defined baseline for comparison.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is evaluated for single- or multiphase solid-solution high-entropy alloys when exposed to temperatures above 900 °C in oxidizing/corrosive environments, without significant secondary phase precipitation that could otherwise alter oxide formation kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Al, Si, and Mn ensuring comparable microstructures. Expose each sample to a controlled oxidizing atmosphere at 950 °C for 100 hours. Characterize the oxide scales using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and measure weight gain kinetics to assess oxide thickness, phase identity, and structural coherence.
measurements: oxide layer thickness and morphology (via SEM)
spallation occurrence and weight gain analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If CrFeCoNiAl samples do not exhibit a significantly more coherent, adherent, and slow-growing protective oxide (predominantly alumina) relative to the CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn baselines, or if oxide cracking/spallation is observed in the CrFeCoNiAl samples at levels comparable to the others, the hypothesis would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the ability to form a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer above 900 °C is governed by the selective oxidation of Cr and certain alloying elements (Si or Al) that form a mixed, adherent oxide. This oxide scale forms by preferential diffusion that enriches the surface with Cr and Si/Al, leading to a coherent, low-defect barrier. In contrast, when X is Mn, the resulting oxide includes more volatile or less coherent manganese oxide phases, which predispose the layer to cracking and spallation.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloy in a single-phase or well-controlled multiphase metallic solid-solution state.
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloy to an oxidative (or corrosive) atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C.
drafts.conditions: High-temperature exposure (>900 °C) in an oxidative environment with controlled oxygen partial pressure; similar exposure durations and ramp rates for each alloy composition.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense, coherent oxide scale enriched in Cr and Si (or Al) with low defect density and strong interfacial bonding.
drafts.mechanism: Preferential oxidation and diffusion yield a surface enrichment of Cr and passivating elements (Si/Al). This results in the nucleation and growth of a mixed Cr-Si-O or Cr-Al-O oxide layer that is slow-growing and mechanically adherent. In contrast, the presence of Mn leads to oxide phases that are less coherent, with structural defects promoting crack propagation and spallation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X=Si or Al are predicted to develop a continuous, adherent, slow-growing oxide layer that resists cracking and spallation; whereas alloys with X=Mn will preferentially form less coherent, defect-prone oxide scales leading to cracking and eventual spallation under the same conditions.
drafts.baseline: The comparison baseline is provided by CrFeCoNiMn alloys, where Mn’s oxidation behavior leads to unstable oxide formation.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies to alloys processed to a homogeneous single-phase or controlled multiphase metallic solid-solution state and tested at temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive service environments mimicking high-temperature operational conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Si, Al, and Mn in a controlled, single-phase metallic solid-solution state. Subject these alloys to identical high-temperature (above 900 °C) oxidative exposures with controlled oxygen partial pressures. Characterize the resulting oxide scales via electron microscopy (scanning and transmission), X-ray diffraction, and elemental mapping (EDS) over defined time intervals.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and growth rate
Microstructural coherence and presence of defects (e.g., cracks or spallation) at the metal–oxide interface
Phase composition of the oxide (identification of mixed Cr-Si-O or Cr-Al-O versus Mn-oxide phases)
Elemental distribution profile across the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with X = Si or Al do not develop a continuous, coherent, and slow-growing oxide scale distinct from the oxide behavior observed in the Mn-containing alloy, or if they display similar cracking and spallation characteristics as the Mn variant, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloys, the nature of the element X governs the formation and stability of a protective oxide layer via selective oxidation kinetics. In particular, when X is Al, its high oxygen affinity promotes the formation of a slow-growing, coherent, alumina-rich sublayer that relieves stresses at the metal/oxide interface, thereby inhibiting cracking and spallation. In contrast, when X is Si or Mn, the oxide scales form either too rapidly or with less beneficial adhesion properties, leading to unstable, spallation‐prone films.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state
drafts.intervention: Substitute X with Al, Si, or Mn and expose the alloy specimens to an oxidative (or corrosive) atmosphere at temperatures above 900°C for prolonged times
drafts.conditions: Exposure at ≥900°C in atmospheric air (or defined oxidative/corrosive environment) over durations sufficient to assess steady-state oxide-scale growth
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation and nature of the surface oxide layer—specifically, the development of an Al-rich (Al2O3) sublayer that is compositionally graded and mechanically coherent with the underlying metal
drafts.mechanism: Selective oxidation: In Al-containing alloys, Al diffuses to the surface and reacts with oxygen to form a thin, slow-growing alumina layer that minimizes growth stresses through better lattice match and adherence. In contrast, alloys where X is Si or Mn lack this beneficial oxidation behavior, leading to thicker, more rapidly growing oxide scales that develop internal stresses and spall.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys with Al will form a thinner, continuous, and adherent alumina-rich oxide layer that remains intact above 900°C, while those with Si or Mn will develop thicker, less coherent scales prone to cracking and spallation.
drafts.baseline: The performance of CrFeCoNiMn or CrFeCoNiSi alloys under the same conditions, which are expected to show unstable oxide layers, serves as the controlled baseline.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state exposed to oxidative or corrosive atmospheres at temperatures above 900°C over periods sufficient for observable scale growth and degradation processes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare and process three sets of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples with X = Al, Si, and Mn under identical conditions. Expose all samples to an oxidative atmosphere at ≥900°C for a fixed time interval. Perform pre- and post-exposure microstructural characterization (using SEM, XRD, and adhesion testing) to evaluate oxide thickness, phase composition, and scale integrity.
measurements: Phase identification (using XRD to detect alumina versus other oxides)
Adhesion/coherence testing of the oxide scale (e.g., via spallation or thermal cycling tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not produce a significantly thinner, more coherent, and stable oxide layer (with less spallation) compared to the Si or Mn-containing alloys, or if the differences are not statistically significant under the defined test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.
